summary: Who? The question of the Heavenly Questions, and of an empty sky.
placement: Chosen by farthest-point sampling on the integrated Burke–Shaw trajectory, so the eight stars spread across its projected shape. 遠 takes the point farthest from the system’s centre, 孤 the most isolated of the rest, and 寂 the point nearest the centre. A design choice, not a claim.

satellites.title: The Heavenly Questions
satellites.evidence: The Tianwen opens: 遂古之初，誰傳道之？上下未形，何由考之 — “of the beginning of the distant past, who has told it? Before above and below had taken form, how could it be examined?” The poem asks well over a hundred questions and answers none.

satellites.title: Two Questions to an Empty Sky
satellites.evidence: Proposed pairing: at lunch at Los Alamos in 1950, Enrico Fermi is reported to have asked “Where is everybody?”: if life is common, why is the sky silent? Rushi sets the question beside the Tianwen. Both ask the sky who is there, and neither has been answered.
satellites.caveat: Fermi’s words are remembered differently by those present (Jones 1985). The pairing with the Tianwen is Rushi’s proposition, not a historical link.
